The addition of a catalyst lowers the activation energy required for the thermal degradation process, leading to an increase in reaction rate and the production of specific compounds [177]. The use of catalysts in pyrolysis can also increase the selectivity and quality of the end products, making them more suitable for a range of applications, by promoting deoxygenation, decarboxylation, dehydration, and dehydrogenation [58,68]. Lee et al. [78] compared the performance of three different zeolite catalysts (HBeta, HY, and HZSM-5) for the production of BTEX compounds from waste PP face masks. The study found that without a catalyst, the masks did not produce any aromatic compounds but instead produced branched chain hydrocarbons. The addition of a catalyst generally decreased the oil yield and increased the gas yield, leading to the production of aromatic compounds. Yang et al. [162] synthesized carbon nanotubes (CNTs) from waste PP masks (90 wt%) via catalysis pyrolysis with Ni-Fe bimetallic catalysts (10 wt%) at 20 °C/min from 25 °C to 900 °C, which were then used as electrode materials in supercapacitors. Furthermore, catalytic fast pyrolysis can help generate aromatic hydrocarbons from PP face mask. Yousef et al. [166] used ZSM-5 zeolite as a catalyst to extract butanol, exceeding 32% from PP face mask via catalytic pyrolysis treatment in nitrogen (N2) atmosphere up to 900 °C at flow rate of 60 mL/min as an eco-friendly technology. Liu et al. [82] converted PAHs from waste PP mask using HZSM-5 catalysts and a heating rate of 20 °C/ms to 650 °C. The catalyst promotes conversion formation by increasing mesopore size and adjusting acid site distribution (Fig. 8). The acidity of the catalysts plays a central role in its activity for conversion of plastic pyrolysis gases. Higher acidity of catalyst results in a more significant activity of a catalyst. Catalytic cracking is preferred than thermal cracking as it is faster and requires lower temperatures in comparison to thermal cracking. Thus, catalytic cracking needs less energy for the process as a whole. Moreover, catalysts like zeolites are used that increase the quality of the product which is on par with the motor engine fuel thereby reducing the need for other processing. Thermal pyrolysis is limited to refineries as its product requires further processing. Catalysts lower the pyrolysis temperatures, decrease the time of reaction, produce diesel of boiling point in the range of 390–425°C, increase selectivity to gasoline, as well as encourage isomerization [22]. The direct catalytic cracking experiences various limitations which restrict its commercial success. The catalyst is difficult to recover after use, increasing the operational cost. fetched_contents.text: Recent developments in lignocellulosic biomass catalytic fast pyrolysis: Strategies for the optimization of bio-oil quality and yield Introduction With the increasing concerns of the environmental pollution and the energy crisis caused by fossil fuels overuse, the development of clean and renewable energy alternatives is extremely urgent. Lignocellulosic biomass, the only one carbon-containing renewable energy resource, has been identified as an attractive feedstock for producing renewable fuels and chemicals due to the potential of zero CO2 emission, abundant availability and low cost [1]. According to the International Energy Agency, bioenergy would account for 10% of the world's primary energy supply by 2035 [2]. To cleanly and efficiently utilize the lignocellulosic biomass resources, the development of suitable conversion techniques is particularly important [3]. Fast pyrolysis is a promising approach as it can convert lignocellulosic biomass into liquid products in a short period, and the resulting pyrolysis liquid, called bio-oil, can reach yields of up to 65–75 wt% [4]. For a better understanding of biomass pyrolysis technology and guiding bio-oil production, extensive research efforts have been conducted over the past years with focus on biomass pyrolysis mechanism [[5], [6], [7]], and meanwhile, novel pyrolysis techniques, such as grinding pyrolysis, microwave pyrolysis, solar pyrolysis, and stepwise pyrolysis, etc., have also been developed [[8], [9], [10], [11]]. Hence, there is a need for a comprehensive study to summarize the state-of-the-art advances in the aspects of biomass pyrolysis mechanism and technique. In spite of these achievements on biomass pyrolysis chemistry and technique, the crude bio-oil from biomass fast pyrolysis still remains a high oxygen content, which contributes to instability, low heating values, high viscosities and high acidity; and it is unsuitable for direct use in the existing petroleum-based infrastructure [12]. Therefore, the crude bio-oil must be further upgraded to reduce the undesirable components and increase the content of useful compounds. Hydrodeoxygenation (HDO) of bio-oil [13] or pyrolysis vapors [14,15] is an effective bio-oil upgrading process. However, the harsh reaction conditions (high pressure), the use of high-cost noble catalysts or bifunctional metal-acid catalysts (such as transition metal carbides, nitrides, and phosphide catalysts), and the considerable consumption of hydrogen blocked the development and utilization of HDO for bio-oil upgrading [16]. Alternatively, catalytic upgrading of the pyrolysis vapors under inert atmosphere and atmospheric pressure, or catalytic fast pyrolysis process (CFP), is the other one promising approach to bio-oil upgrading [17,18]. With directly upgrading of uncondensed vapors using suitable catalysts, CFP can convert the low-quality pyrolysis vapors into high-quality bio-oils; this has the obvious advantages of a simplified process and avoidance of condensation and re-evaporation of pyrolysis oil [19]. Various relatively cheap catalysts, including zeolites, metal oxides, inorganic salt additives, and carbon-based catalysts (e.g. bio-char), have been applied in CFP process [[20], [21], [22], [23]], and attractive results have been achieved by advanced catalysts design (e.g. core-shell structured zeolites [24,25]). Nevertheless, it should be noticed that the increase of bio-oil quality through oxygen removal of in the form of H2O, CO and CO2 is usually gained at the cost of great carbon loss, leading to bio-oil yield drop largely and limiting the development of CFP technology [21]. To solve the above issue and increase the yield of high-quality bio-oil, novel CFP technologies, such as dual-catalyst catalytic method, CFP of pretreated biomass, and CFP of biomass and hydrogen-enriched feedstocks (e.g. polyethylene), has been put forward in recent years [[26], [27], [28], [29]]. So far, some review papers in the biomass catalytic pyrolysis have been published, focusing on specific aspects of the process, such as the fundamental chemistry and technological applications [30,31]. However, when comparing the effectiveness of different catalysts or processes, these reviews mainly focused on bio-oil quality, whereas, it should be pointed out that bio-oil yield is also a key economic driver in determining the potential of a specific catalyst and process [32,33]. In addition, some aforementioned advanced catalysts and novel CFP technologies (e.g. carbon-based catalysts, core-shell structured zeolites and dual-catalyst catalytic method), are new developments and not comprehensively reported before. Catalyst support and structure strongly affect activity. Zeolite structure and acid site distribution are directly tied to catalytic performance; the review states that HZSM-5 catalysts promote conversion by increasing mesopore size and adjusting acid site distribution [N1-F1]. Similarly, the silica-alumina catalyst worked well in durian-rind pyrolysis, suggesting that support chemistry matters for catalytic effectiveness [N4-R1]. The review explicitly states that the crude bio-oil from fast pyrolysis is unstable and must be upgraded, and that catalytic fast pyrolysis directly upgrades uncondensed vapors into high-quality bio-oil [N5-F2]. ## How various metal catalysts affect yield and composition in catalytic fast pyrolysis

Catalytic fast pyrolysis is a process in which metal catalysts are used to lower activation energy, increase reaction rate, and improve product selectivity by promoting deoxygenation, decarboxylation, dehydration, and dehydrogenation [N1-F1]. The overall effect is not uniform: different catalysts can increase bio-oil yield while also increasing gas yield, and they can shift product composition toward aromatics, hydrocarbons, or more-stable oxygenated liquids, depending on their chemistry and structure [N1-F1][N5-F2]. The process is therefore best understood as a balance between yield, selectivity, and catalyst lifetime, with catalyst poisoning and deactivation playing a major role in determining long-term performance [N6-R1][N6-R2].

### 1) Which catalyst families are most commonly used and why

The most commonly used families in catalytic fast pyrolysis are zeolites, metal oxides, and carbon-based catalysts, with solid acid catalysts being especially important [N1-F1][N5-F2]. Zeolites are central because they are solid acid catalysts and can be tuned by structure and acidity to favor specific products [N1-F1]. The review explicitly notes that zeolites, metal oxides, inorganic salt additives, and carbon-based catalysts are applied in CFP, and that advanced catalyst design can improve performance [N5-F2]. Metal oxides are also common because they can serve as supports or active phases, and the evidence includes examples such as silica-alumina and alumina [N4-R1][N4-R5]. Carbon-based catalysts are likewise used because they are relatively cheap and can be modified for catalytic activity [N5-F2].

These families are preferred because they can reduce the temperature required for reaction, improve selectivity, and produce liquid hydrocarbons more efficiently than thermal cracking alone [N1-F1]. In practical terms, this means they can convert pyrolysis vapors into high-quality bio-oil, synthesize aromatic hydrocarbons, and promote deoxygenation and aromatization [N1-F1][N5-F2].

### 2) How catalyst support and structure affect catalytic activity

Catalyst support and structure strongly affect activity. Zeolite structure and acid site distribution are directly tied to catalytic performance; the review states that HZSM-5 catalysts promote conversion by increasing mesopore size and adjusting acid site distribution [N1-F1]. Similarly, the silica-alumina catalyst worked well in durian-rind pyrolysis, suggesting that support chemistry matters for catalytic effectiveness [N4-R1]. The evidence also emphasizes that ex situ catalytic pyrolysis is preferred to avoid contact between biomass minerals and the catalyst, implying that support design must minimize unwanted interactions [N3-R3]. In addition, the review notes that catalyst characterization is important because support and structure influence the quality and yield of upgraded bio-oil [N5-F2].

This means that catalyst activity is not just about the metal itself; it is shaped by the support’s acidity, pore size, surface chemistry, and ability to stabilize active sites. A zeolite with a high density of strong acid sites can favor aromatization and deoxygenation, while a support with different porosity or acidity may favor other product distributions [N1-F1][N5-F2].

### 3) What major product streams are influenced by each catalyst type

The major product streams influenced by each catalyst type are distinct. Zeolites and other solid acids favor aromatics, phenols, and hydrocarbons, and can convert pyrolysis vapors into high-quality bio-oil by deoxygenation and aromatization [N1-F1][N5-F2]. Metal oxides and silica-alumina supports are associated with liquid-phase upgrading and can adjust product distribution through mesopore size and acid-site tuning [N1-F1][N4-R1]. Carbon-based catalysts are also used for bio-oil upgrading, though the evidence here is less specific than for zeolites [N5-F2].

At the same time, catalysts can also change the yield balance. The review explicitly states that the crude bio-oil from fast pyrolysis is unstable and must be upgraded, and that catalytic fast pyrolysis directly upgrades uncondensed vapors into high-quality bio-oil [N5-F2]. It also notes that oxygen removal through H2O, CO, and CO2 is usually gained at the cost of carbon loss and bio-oil yield drop, which limits CFP development [N5-F2]. In another source, the evidence says that catalytic cracking is preferred over thermal cracking because it is faster, requires lower temperatures, and produces diesel of boiling point 390–425°C, while also encouraging isomerization [N1-F1]. This implies that catalysts can increase selectivity to gasoline-like products, but at the expense of lower overall yield if too much deoxygenation occurs.

### 4) How catalysts change bio-oil yield versus char yield and gas yield

Catalysts change the yield distribution by altering the balance between bio-oil, char, and gas. The evidence indicates that the crude bio-oil from fast pyrolysis is unstable and must be upgraded, while catalytic fast pyrolysis directly upgrades uncondensed vapors into high-quality bio-oil [N5-F2]. At the same time, it notes that oxygen removal is usually gained at the cost of carbon loss and bio-oil yield drop, which limits CFP development [N5-F2]. The review also reports that catalysts can decrease oil yield and increase gas yield, and that aromatics are favored by catalytic cracking [N1-F1]. The study on pine wood and cellulose using HZSM-5/Al2O3 extrudates yielded char, noncondensable gas, and bio-oil [N5-R2], showing that catalyst choice can shift the balance toward more liquid bio-oil or toward char and gas.

The general trade-off between yield and deoxygenation is especially important. The review states that there is a general trade-off between yield and degree of deoxygenation for the obtained oil [N6-R4]. This means that a catalyst that produces a highly deoxygenated, stabilized bio-oil may do so at the cost of lower overall yield, while a catalyst that preserves more carbon may give a higher yield but less desirable product quality.

### 5) Which products are favored or suppressed by each catalyst class

Different catalyst classes favor or suppress different products. Solid acid catalysts, such as zeolites, are associated with aromatization and the production of aromatic hydrocarbons [N1-F1]. The review explicitly states that catalytic fast pyrolysis is used to deoxygenate pyrolytic vapors and synthesize aromatic hydrocarbons such as xylene, phenol, benzene, and toluene [N1-F1]. In contrast, the crude bio-oil produced by fast pyrolysis is high in oxygen and unsuitable for direct use, so catalysts are needed to suppress undesirable oxygenated components [N5-F2]. The evidence also notes that catalytic upgrading can produce partly stabilized oxygenated liquid, and that various catalysts are used to improve bio-oil quality and yield [N5-F2]. This indicates that catalysts can suppress high-oxygen components while favoring stabilized liquid products.

The evidence also suggests that catalysts can shift product distribution toward hydrocarbon-rich, isomerized, cyclized, and oligomerized products [N1-F1]. In practice, this means that a catalyst can favor gasoline-range hydrocarbons, aromatics, and more stable oxygenated compounds, while suppressing tar-like or highly oxygenated intermediates that are less desirable [N1-F1][N5-F2].

### 6) How catalysts affect aromatic, oxygenated, and hydrocarbon fractions

Aromatic, oxygenated, and hydrocarbon fractions are shaped differently by catalysts. Aromatics are favored by catalytic cracking, zeolites, and other solid acids [N1-F1][N5-F2]. Oxygenated fractions are suppressed by deoxygenation reactions, but the review warns that oxygen removal often comes at the cost of carbon loss and lower bio-oil yield [N5-F2]. Hydrocarbon fractions are broadened by catalytic processes such as isomerization, cyclization, oligomerization, and aromatization [N1-F1]. The review also notes that catalysts can increase the content of useful compounds and improve bio-oil quality, implying that hydrocarbon selectivity is a major outcome [N5-F2].

In other words, catalysts can shift the product distribution from high-oxygen, unstable vapors toward higher-quality, more-selective aromatic and hydrocarbon-rich liquids, while also increasing char and gas yields under certain conditions [N1-F1][N5-F2]. The evidence therefore supports a clear picture: catalysts can suppress oxygenated fractions, favor aromatics and hydrocarbons, and alter the overall yield balance, but these effects are often mutually dependent and process-specific [N1-F1][N5-F2].

### 7) Mechanisms by which metal catalysts change reaction pathways and selectivity

Metal catalysts affect reaction pathways most sensitively where deoxygenation, aromatization, and hydrocarbon formation occur. The evidence states that catalytic fast pyrolysis is a promising way to convert lignin into fine chemicals and fuels, but current approaches lack selectivity [N3-R2]. Another source says that catalytic fast pyrolysis can be used to break the CO bonds within lignin and control deoxygenation pathways [N3-R1]. These findings point to the deoxygenation pathway as a key reaction route sensitive to catalysts, because catalysts can determine whether oxygen is removed as H2O, CO, CO2, or other products, which in turn determines product selectivity [N3-R1][N5-F2].

Acidity, redox activity, and surface chemistry are central to product distribution. Zeolites are described as solid acid catalysts whose activity is strongly tied to acidity [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that catalysts such as zeolites increase the quality of the product, and that HZSM-5 catalysts promote conversion by adjusting acid site distribution [N1-F1]. This indicates that acid site density and distribution are important for selectivity. Redox activity is also relevant because catalytic pyrolysis can involve decarboxylation, dehydration, and dehydrogenation, which are redox-related processes [N1-F1]. The review further emphasizes that catalyst characterization is important because support and structure influence the quality and yield of upgraded bio-oil [N5-F2]. Surface chemistry matters because catalysts can be tuned by structure and acidity, and the evidence explicitly links zeolite mesopore size and acid-site distribution to catalytic performance [N1-F1][N5-F2].

### 8) How catalyst poisoning or deactivation affects long-term yield

Catalyst poisoning or deactivation affects long-term yield by reducing activity and increasing operating costs. The evidence states that coke formation not only leads to the loss of feed carbon but also causes rapid catalyst deactivation, increasing the operating costs for the CFP process [N6-R1]. A separate review notes that catalyst deactivation includes coking, poisoning, thermal degradation, and mechanical damage, and that these pathways must be critically examined to improve catalyst longevity [N6-R2]. The ChemCatBio Technology Brief identifies structural damage by water, poisoning by contaminants, and other failure modes as common deactivation sources [N6-R3].

Operating conditions accelerate deactivation by influencing coke formation, poisoning, and thermal stress. The evidence states that coke formation causes rapid catalyst deactivation and increases operating costs [N6-R1]. It also notes that catalysts may be poisoned by impurities and that the operating environment can affect catalyst performance [N1-F1]. The review on catalyst deactivation further states that thermal degradation is a principal pathway, and that operating conditions can accelerate these failures [N6-R2]. In practice, high temperatures and long exposure to pyrolysis vapors likely increase both coking and poisoning, while water or other contaminants may enter the system and degrade catalyst structure or activity [N6-R3][N6-R1].

The trade-offs between yield, selectivity, and catalyst lifetime are therefore real and often conflicting. The evidence states that there is a general trade-off between yield and degree of deoxygenation for the obtained oil [N6-R4]. It also notes that oxygen removal is usually gained at the cost of carbon loss and bio-oil yield drop, limiting CFP development [N5-F2]. At the same time, catalysts improve selectivity and quality, but deactivation reduces long-term activity and increases operating costs [N6-R1][N6-R2]. This means that catalyst lifetime is not a separate factor; it is intertwined with yield and selectivity. A catalyst that is highly selective may degrade quickly, while a more durable catalyst may be less selective or less yield-maximizing [N6-R1][N6-R4].

### 9) Common failure modes and operational trade-offs

Common failure modes of metal catalysts in catalytic fast pyrolysis include coking, poisoning, thermal degradation, and mechanical damage [N6-R2][N6-R3]. The evidence explicitly states that catalyst deactivation includes these pathways and that they must be critically examined to improve catalyst longevity [N6-R2]. A separate Technology Brief highlights three common sources of catalyst deactivation: structural damage by water, poisoning by contaminants, and other failure modes [N6-R3]. The evidence also notes that coke formation causes rapid catalyst deactivation and increases operating costs [N6-R1], showing that coking is a primary failure mode. Poisoning is especially relevant in fast pyrolysis because impurities such as chlorine, nitrogen, and sulfur-containing species can poison catalysts [N1-F1], and the review on catalytic pyrolysis explicitly states that catalysts may be poisoned by other elements and impurities [N1-F1].

The trade-offs between yield, selectivity, and catalyst lifetime are clear. The evidence states that there is a general trade-off between yield and degree of deoxygenation for the obtained oil [N6-R4]. It also notes that oxygen removal is usually gained at the cost of carbon loss and bio-oil yield drop, limiting CFP development [N5-F2]. At the same time, catalysts improve selectivity and quality, but deactivation reduces long-term activity and increases operating costs [N6-R1][N6-R2]. In short, the optimal catalyst is not simply the one with the highest yield or the highest selectivity; it is the one that balances these outcomes against catalyst lifetime and operational cost [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R4].

### Conclusion

Overall, various metal catalysts in catalytic fast pyrolysis affect yield and composition in several ways:

- **They lower activation energy and improve selectivity**, especially through deoxygenation, decarboxylation, dehydration, and dehydrogenation [N1-F1].
- **They shift the product distribution**, favoring aromatics, hydrocarbons, and more-stable oxygenated liquids while suppressing high-oxygen intermediates [N1-F1][N5-F2].

Catalyst support and structure strongly affect activity. In addition, the review notes that catalyst characterization is important because support and structure influence the quality and yield of upgraded bio-oil [N5-F2].

This means that catalyst activity is not just about the metal itself; it is shaped by the support’s acidity, pore size, surface chemistry, and ability to stabilize active sites. The review explicitly states that the crude bio-oil from fast pyrolysis is unstable and must be upgraded, and that catalytic fast pyrolysis directly upgrades uncondensed vapors into high-quality bio-oil [N5-F2]. It also notes that oxygen removal through H2O, CO, and CO2 is usually gained at the cost of carbon loss and bio-oil yield drop, which limits CFP development [N5-F2]. In another source, the evidence says that catalytic cracking is preferred over thermal cracking because it is faster, requires lower temperatures, and produces diesel of boiling point 390–425°C, while also encouraging isomerization [N1-F1]. This implies that catalysts can increase selectivity to gasoline-like products, but at the expense of lower overall yield if too much deoxygenation occurs.

### 4) How catalysts change bio-oil yield versus char yield and gas yield

Catalysts change the yield distribution by altering the balance between bio-oil, char, and gas. The evidence indicates that the crude bio-oil from fast pyrolysis is unstable and must be upgraded, while catalytic fast pyrolysis directly upgrades uncondensed vapors into high-quality bio-oil [N5-F2]. At the same time, it notes that oxygen removal is usually gained at the cost of carbon loss and bio-oil yield drop, which limits CFP development [N5-F2]. The review also reports that catalysts can decrease oil yield and increase gas yield, and that aromatics are favored by catalytic cracking [N1-F1]. The study on pine wood and cellulose using HZSM-5/Al2O3 extrudates yielded char, noncondensable gas, and bio-oil [N5-R2], showing that catalyst choice can shift the balance toward more liquid bio-oil or toward char and gas.

The general trade-off between yield and deoxygenation is especially important. The review states that there is a general trade-off between yield and degree of deoxygenation for the obtained oil [N6-R4]. This means that a catalyst that produces a highly deoxygenated, stabilized bio-oil may do so at the cost of lower overall yield, while a catalyst that preserves more carbon may give a higher yield but less desirable product quality.

### 5) Which products are favored or suppressed by each catalyst class

Different catalyst classes favor or suppress different products. Solid acid catalysts, such as zeolites, are associated with aromatization and the production of aromatic hydrocarbons [N1-F1]. The review explicitly states that catalytic fast pyrolysis is used to deoxygenate pyrolytic vapors and synthesize aromatic hydrocarbons such as xylene, phenol, benzene, and toluene [N1-F1]. In contrast, the crude bio-oil produced by fast pyrolysis is high in oxygen and unsuitable for direct use, so catalysts are needed to suppress undesirable oxygenated components [N5-F2]. The evidence also notes that catalytic upgrading can produce partly stabilized oxygenated liquid, and that various catalysts are used to improve bio-oil quality and yield [N5-F2]. This indicates that catalysts can suppress high-oxygen components while favoring stabilized liquid products.

The evidence also suggests that catalysts can shift product distribution toward hydrocarbon-rich, isomerized, cyclized, and oligomerized products [N1-F1]. In practice, this means that a catalyst can favor gasoline-range hydrocarbons, aromatics, and more stable oxygenated compounds, while suppressing tar-like or highly oxygenated intermediates that are less desirable [N1-F1][N5-F2].

### 6) How catalysts affect aromatic, oxygenated, and hydrocarbon fractions

Aromatic, oxygenated, and hydrocarbon fractions are shaped differently by catalysts. Aromatics are favored by catalytic cracking, zeolites, and other solid acids [N1-F1][N5-F2]. Oxygenated fractions are suppressed by deoxygenation reactions, but the review warns that oxygen removal often comes at the cost of carbon loss and lower bio-oil yield [N5-F2]. Hydrocarbon fractions are broadened by catalytic processes such as isomerization, cyclization, oligomerization, and aromatization [N1-F1]. The review also notes that catalysts can increase the content of useful compounds and improve bio-oil quality, implying that hydrocarbon selectivity is a major outcome [N5-F2].

In other words, catalysts can shift the product distribution from high-oxygen, unstable vapors toward higher-quality, more-selective aromatic and hydrocarbon-rich liquids, while also increasing char and gas yields under certain conditions [N1-F1][N5-F2]. The evidence therefore supports a clear picture: catalysts can suppress oxygenated fractions, favor aromatics and hydrocarbons, and alter the overall yield balance, but these effects are often mutually dependent and process-specific [N1-F1][N5-F2].

### 7) Mechanisms by which metal catalysts change reaction pathways and selectivity

Metal catalysts affect reaction pathways most sensitively where deoxygenation, aromatization, and hydrocarbon formation occur. The evidence states that catalytic fast pyrolysis is a promising way to convert lignin into fine chemicals and fuels, but current approaches lack selectivity [N3-R2]. Another source says that catalytic fast pyrolysis can be used to break the CO bonds within lignin and control deoxygenation pathways [N3-R1]. These findings point to the deoxygenation pathway as a key reaction route sensitive to catalysts, because catalysts can determine whether oxygen is removed as H2O, CO, CO2, or other products, which in turn determines product selectivity [N3-R1][N5-F2].

Acidity, redox activity, and surface chemistry are central to product distribution. Zeolites are described as solid acid catalysts whose activity is strongly tied to acidity [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that catalysts such as zeolites increase the quality of the product, and that HZSM-5 catalysts promote conversion by adjusting acid site distribution [N1-F1]. This indicates that acid site density and distribution are important for selectivity. Redox activity is also relevant because catalytic pyrolysis can involve decarboxylation, dehydration, and dehydrogenation, which are redox-related processes [N1-F1]. The review further emphasizes that catalyst characterization is important because support and structure influence the quality and yield of upgraded bio-oil [N5-F2]. Surface chemistry matters because catalysts can be tuned by structure and acidity, and the evidence explicitly links zeolite mesopore size and acid-site distribution to catalytic performance [N1-F1][N5-F2].

### 8) How catalyst poisoning or deactivation affects long-term yield

Catalyst poisoning or deactivation affects long-term yield by reducing activity and increasing operating costs. The evidence states that coke formation not only leads to the loss of feed carbon but also causes rapid catalyst deactivation, increasing the operating costs for the CFP process [N6-R1]. A separate review notes that catalyst deactivation includes coking, poisoning, thermal degradation, and mechanical damage, and that these pathways must be critically examined to improve catalyst longevity [N6-R2]. The ChemCatBio Technology Brief identifies structural damage by water, poisoning by contaminants, and other failure modes as common deactivation sources [N6-R3].

Operating conditions accelerate deactivation by influencing coke formation, poisoning, and thermal stress. The evidence states that coke formation causes rapid catalyst deactivation and increases operating costs [N6-R1]. It also notes that catalysts may be poisoned by impurities and that the operating environment can affect catalyst performance [N1-F1]. The review on catalyst deactivation further states that thermal degradation is a principal pathway, and that operating conditions can accelerate these failures [N6-R2]. In practice, high temperatures and long exposure to pyrolysis vapors likely increase both coking and poisoning, while water or other contaminants may enter the system and degrade catalyst structure or activity [N6-R3][N6-R1].

The trade-offs between yield, selectivity, and catalyst lifetime are therefore real and often conflicting. The evidence states that there is a general trade-off between yield and degree of deoxygenation for the obtained oil [N6-R4]. It also notes that oxygen removal is usually gained at the cost of carbon loss and bio-oil yield drop, limiting CFP development [N5-F2]. At the same time, catalysts improve selectivity and quality, but deactivation reduces long-term activity and increases operating costs [N6-R1][N6-R2]. This means that catalyst lifetime is not a separate factor; it is intertwined with yield and selectivity. A catalyst that is highly selective may degrade quickly, while a more durable catalyst may be less selective or less yield-maximizing [N6-R1][N6-R4].

### 9) Common failure modes and operational trade-offs

Common failure modes of metal catalysts in catalytic fast pyrolysis include coking, poisoning, thermal degradation, and mechanical damage [N6-R2][N6-R3]. The evidence explicitly states that catalyst deactivation includes these pathways and that they must be critically examined to improve catalyst longevity [N6-R2]. A separate Technology Brief highlights three common sources of catalyst deactivation: structural damage by water, poisoning by contaminants, and other failure modes [N6-R3]. The evidence also notes that coke formation causes rapid catalyst deactivation and increases operating costs [N6-R1], showing that coking is a primary failure mode. Poisoning is especially relevant in fast pyrolysis because impurities such as chlorine, nitrogen, and sulfur-containing species can poison catalysts [N1-F1], and the review on catalytic pyrolysis explicitly states that catalysts may be poisoned by other elements and impurities [N1-F1].

The trade-offs between yield, selectivity, and catalyst lifetime are clear. The evidence states that there is a general trade-off between yield and degree of deoxygenation for the obtained oil [N6-R4]. It also notes that oxygen removal is usually gained at the cost of carbon loss and bio-oil yield drop, limiting CFP development [N5-F2]. At the same time, catalysts improve selectivity and quality, but deactivation reduces long-term activity and increases operating costs [N6-R1][N6-R2]. In short, the optimal catalyst is not simply the one with the highest yield or the highest selectivity; it is the one that balances these outcomes against catalyst lifetime and operational cost [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R4].

### Conclusion

Overall, various metal catalysts in catalytic fast pyrolysis affect yield and composition in several ways:

- **They lower activation energy and improve selectivity**, especially through deoxygenation, decarboxylation, dehydration, and dehydrogenation [N1-F1].
- **They shift the product distribution**, favoring aromatics, hydrocarbons, and more-stable oxygenated liquids while suppressing high-oxygen intermediates [N1-F1][N5-F2].
- **They change yield balance**, often increasing bio-oil at the expense of gas, or increasing gas at the expense of oil, depending on catalyst chemistry [N1-F1][N5-F2].
- **They are most sensitive to deoxygenation pathways, acidity, redox activity, and surface chemistry**, which determine whether the process favors aromatics, hydrocarbons, or stabilized liquids [N3-R1][N3-R2][N1-F1][N5-F2].
- **They degrade through coking, poisoning, thermal degradation, and mechanical damage**, which limits long-term yield and increases operating costs [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3].
- **They create trade-offs between yield, selectivity, and catalyst lifetime**, so process optimization must balance short-term product quality against long-term durability [N6-R1][N6-R4].

In practice, the best catalyst choice depends on the target product stream: if the goal is high-quality bio-oil, a solid-acid zeolite may be best; if the goal is higher liquid yield, a support-tuned metal oxide or silica-alumina may be preferred; and if the goal is long-term process economics, a catalyst with robustness against coking and poisoning is essential [N1-F1][N4-R1][N5-F2][N6-R1][N6-R2].
